messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Gaussian processes
parts:
I just added a 10-page chapter to the manual on coding
Gaussian processes. I start with a simple Stan model that
samples from the prior, discuss a Cholesky transform for
efficient multivariate Gaussian generation, extend it to obvious joint model
that can compute the posterior, then to hyperparameter estimation,
then I unfold it with the analytical posterior. I also do logistic
regression. So it's quite a few models. I tested them all
on simulated data.

The examples are in src/models/misc/gaussian-process
and I included R code to generate the data and also run
the examples in Rstan.

It all works surprisingly well, at least up to a few
hundred dimensions. And it's pretty easy to code in Stan.
(Seeing Yuanjun's code for Andrew's class really helped!)

One issue I was wondering about is how to code the linear
algebra most effectively. The sources I read (Neal, Rasmussen
and Williams, and MacKay) all do it differently from each other
and from the way I did it.

K: M x N
C: N x N, pos def
y: N x 1
W: M x M

posterior mean: K' * inv(C) * y

posterior covar: W - K' * inv(C) * K

One approach (what you see from Radford), is to compute

inv(C) * y = inv(LL') * y

= L' \ L \ y

I did this the other way around, computing

K' * inv(C) = K / L / L'

so that I could reuse the computation.

Should I be doing it the other way? I wouldn't think
it would really matter much because the Cholesky
factorization should dominate on any sizable problem
and the auto-dif on anything smaller. (These will go
lots faster when I add the partials for matrix division.)

We could add a gaussian_process_sq_exp_log() function
that takes a parameterization of a squared exponential.
Something like this for the prior:

real gaussian_process_sq_exp_log(vector y, vector x,
real eta_sq, real rho_sq, real sigma_sq);

and this for the posterior:

real gaussian_process_sq_exp_log(vector y_tilde, vector x_tilde,
vector y, vector x,
real eta_sq, real rho_sq, real sigma_sq);

And we could do the same for the logistic case, though there's
no good analytic optimization for the posterior. (There are on
the other hand, a whole lot of approximate methods.)

- Bob

K: M x N

  posterior mean:    K' * inv(C) * y

One approach (what you see from Radford), is to compute

   inv(C) * y = inv(LL') * y

              = L' \ L \ y

I did this the other way around, computing

  K' * inv(C) = K / L / L'

so that I could reuse the computation.

Should I be doing it the other way?  I wouldn't think
it would really matter much because the Cholesky

and the auto-dif on anything smaller.  (These will go

It shouldn't matter too much.  Since K' * inv(C) is needed if you want the covar as well your way is probably faster.  Sometimes people only want the posterior mean, in which case the other way is significantly faster.

A big optimization from the AD perspective will be implementing the derivatives of log(det(A)) directly.

We could add a gaussian_process_sq_exp_log() function
that takes a parameterization of a squared exponential.
Something like this for the prior:

  real gaussian_process_sq_exp_log(vector y, vector x,
                                   real eta_sq, real rho_sq, real sigma_sq);

and this for the posterior:

   real gaussian_process_sq_exp_log(vector y_tilde, vector x_tilde,
                                    vector y, vector x,
                                    real eta_sq, real rho_sq, real sigma_sq);

I'd suggest splitting the kernel away from the posterior computation.  E.G., 

matrix sq_exp_kernel(vector x, ...);

And  

real gaussian_process_log(vector y, matrix K, ...);

so that people can easily create new kernels and mix and match them.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Gaussian processes

On Wednesday, January 16, 2013 2:50:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I just added a 10-page chapter to the manual on coding
Gaussian processes.  I start with a simple Stan model that
samples from the prior, discuss a Cholesky transform for
efficient multivariate Gaussian generation, extend it to obvious joint model
that can compute the posterior, then to hyperparameter estimation,
then I unfold it with the analytical posterior.  I also do logistic
regression.  So it's quite a few models.  I tested them all
on simulated data.

One thing I would add is that in the case where the covariance matrix is fixed, then calculating the Cholesky factorization once and using multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L) only gets you part way to optimum speed because although L is a constant, the inverse of L is calculated repeatedly inside multi_normal_cholesky (except not literally due to the triangular solving). To get optimum speed, you would want to invert L once, transpose that, and do something like this in the model block

lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * dot_self(tL_inv * (y - mu));

But when the covariance matrix is a function of unknown hyperparameters, it doesn't make any difference whether you do multi_normal() or multi_normal_cholesky(). Supporting --- or perhaps even providing convenience functions that implement --- various covariance or correlation functions would be nice, although some of them involve special functions that are not implemented in Stan yet and may or may not be in Boost yet.

Ben

The squared exponential is, by far, the most popular kernel so making it fast is a good thing.  That said, discrete data and people working with non-stationary data  will require different kernels or will use combinations of kernels.  Plus, some will want to use ARD, others won't.  There's a lot of variety out there in how people use GP kernels.

That said, do you think there's a lot to be gained in terms of speed by having such a specialized function?

Michael B's been adding special functions that he needed

I spend all my time using gaussian processes with MCMC.

It is quite surprising where the time is spent. Constructing K and C can be a bottleneck in some cases.

Realising what is dependent and independent on x (the current position) is vital, and storing intermediate vectors of things which are independent of x.

I don;t have time to understand Bob's notation, but my guess is that K is dependent on x and inv(C) * y is independent. So most of the work will be spent in repeatedly contsructing K, little work is done in cholesky factorisation or back substitution, at least for the mean. The variance does need repeated back substitutions.

Of course, to calculate

one should calculate

P = L \ K

and then construct

P' * P

There are as many varieties of gaussian processes as there are names. Surrogate, proxy, linear bayes, estimator, radial basis function, etc etc.

There are many flavours of the algorithms. I come more from a linear bayes perspective. I also pay significant attention to a linear regreassion model as a starting point, with second order terms. I use sophisticated techniques to determine the efficient terms in the polynomial.

There are issues such as whether one should include the variance of the regression beta coefficients on the variance.

I actually use Matern correlation functions rather than gaussian. They are more flexible but more time consuming, unless (as i do) you use approximate methods. Taking the derivatives of matern adds extra complexity...

There is another range of choices in the hyperparameters, you can go from one global correlation length to adapting every term in the correlation matrix - but rasmussen discusses these alternatives quite well.

As a point of note, I caculate all the derivatives and use NUTS very successfully.

A lot (all?) of the computation can be easily vectorised. This is where R is excellent, at things like matrix * matrix calculations. I don;t know exactly what underlying libraries they use, but some version of BLAS must be there. A C implementation should use similar libraries.

We don't pay anything for vectorized vs. unvectorized
loops because Stan loops are compiled to C++ loops.

Having said that, we're using the Eigen C++ lib, which
indeed does efficient matrix ops and linear algebra.

The big deal for us is vectorizing things that involve
the gradient (that is, involve estimated parameters),
because they can dramatically cut down on virtual function
calls, memory fiddling (we manage our own in an arena-based
arrangement), and the size of the expression graph.

- Bob

Maybe we are talking with different ssumptions, but....

I am talking about sampling a single Gaussian process using MCMC.

So if we have nS samples, for the mean we do cholesky factorisation 1 time, we construct the k matrix nS times, and we multiply the K matrix by the stored constant vector nS times.

The K matrix takes nData x dimension operations.

So in total the K matrix contruction dominates, it take O(S x dimension x data points) operations.

That is for the mean. The variance is different, of course, you have to do a lot of back substitutions, but again factorisation is only done once for all samples.

Maybe you are talking about optimising the hyper parameters, where of course you have to factorise each time they change.

It is late and i am tired so I may be wrong, I have not checked against my code, but more likely we are talking about different things. If in doubt I can send some profiling results.

No worries --- I've got it all implemented and
it's easy to see in Stan where the time's going
to go.

There are several different models with different
costs and factorizations. There's the plain
old simulation, hyperparameter estimation,
and joint (or marginal) predictive inference. And
then the same things again with a logistic model for
binary data (or generalized to K-way classification
data).

For Stan, a big cost comes in auto-diff for the
hyperparameter estimation, which we need for HMC/NUTS.

- Bob

>
> I am talking about sampling a single Gaussian process using MCMC.
>
> So if we have nS samples, for the mean we do cholesky factorisation 1 time, we construct the k matrix nS times, and we multiply the K matrix by the stored constant vector nS times.
>
> The K matrix takes nData x dimension operations.
>
> So in total the K matrix contruction dominates, it take O(S x dimension x data points) operations.

Hyperarameter estimation is a subject in itself, there are papers giving the complcated formulae for the derivative of the likelihood function (if doing maximum likelihood evaluation), and other papers taking a bayesian approach to estimation.

Take a look at the www.mucm.ac.uk web site. Technical papers 09/05 and 11/03 may be of interest.
